summary:
The cephalic index is the width of the head expressed as a percentage of its length, the standard measure used to describe head shape in anthropology, paediatrics and ergonomics. It returns cephalic index, width to length ratio, head width (biparietal) and head length (fronto-occipital), and the panel shows all of them at once.

Enter the two diameters and it returns the index together with the shape category the value falls into. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cephalic Index
sections.html:
Cephalic index = (head width ÷ head length) × 100

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
widthmaximum transverse diametermm
lengthmaximum anteroposterior diametermm
indexwidth as a percentage of length%

Where the relationship comes from. Boundaries follow the conventional anthropometric classification (Retzius, 1842; modern cut-offs in Martin & Saller).

sections.title: How do I use the Cephalic Index?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Measure head width across the widest part of the skull, above the ears.
  2. Measure head length from the brow ridge to the furthest point at the back.
  3. Enter both in the same unit — the index is dimensionless, so millimetres or centimetres both work, but never one of each.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Substituting them into the formula gives cephalic index of 78.95%, width to length ratio of 0.7895, head width (biparietal) of 150 mm, head length (fronto-occipital) of 190 mm.

A head 150 mm wide and 190 mm long gives 78.9 — mesocephalic, the middle of the usual adult range.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
below 75Dolichocephaliclong and narrow head
75 – 79.9Mesocephalicaverage, the usual human range
80 – 84.9Brachycephalicshort and broad head
85 and aboveHyperbrachycephalicmarkedly broad head

  • The index describes shape, not size, and it is normal for it to differ between populations and between men and women within the same population.

  • In infants the index is naturally higher, because the skull is still broad relative to its length; adult bands do not apply before about two years of age.

  • Ergonomics uses the same number to size helmets and headphones, where the length matters more than the index itself.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Mixing units: 150 mm of width with 19 cm of length gives an index ten times too small.
  • Using head circumference as the width or the length. Circumference is a different measure and cannot be substituted into this ratio.
  • Treating a high index as a diagnosis. Brachycephaly is a shape, and only a clinician can say whether a particular skull shape is a medical finding.

faq.q: Is the cephalic index the same as the cranial index?
faq.a: Yes in everyday use. Strictly, the cranial index is measured on the skull and the cephalic index on the living head, which is a few millimetres wider because of soft tissue.

faq.q: What is a normal cephalic index?
faq.a: Between about 75 and 85 for adults of most populations. Values outside that range are common in some regions and are not by themselves abnormal.

faq.q: What does the Cephalic Index actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns cephalic index, width to length ratio, head width (biparietal) and head length (fronto-occipital). Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
